case.case_title: Visuvalingam and Others v. Liyanage and Others
case.source_citation: Sri Lanka Law Reports [1984] 2 Sri L.R.

clause.text: Every person has the right to apply to the Supreme Court for violations of fundamental rights.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the petitioners, as readers and contributors of the Saturday Review, had locus standi to apply to the Supreme Court under Article 17 for alleged violations of their fundamental rights due to the banning of the newspaper.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioners claimed that as readers and contributors they had the right to seek relief under Article 17 for violation of their fundamental rights to equality and freedom of speech and expression.
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents argued that the ban was directed at the printers, publishers, and distributors, not the readers or contributors, and that the petitioners lacked locus standi to bring the application under Article 17.
key_facts: The Saturday Review was banned by orders under Emergency Regulations.
The petitioners were readers and one contributor, not the publishers or printers.
Previous applications by the publishers were dismissed for lack of locus standi.
The Court had to decide if readers and contributors have standing to claim violation of fundamental rights due to the ban.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court recognized that the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression includes the freedom of the recipient of information. Therefore, readers and contributors have locus standi to seek relief under Article 17. However, this right is subject to the same restrictions under Article 15(7). The Court also noted that the publisher was a non-citizen company and thus had no fundamental right to publish, which affected the standing of readers indirectly.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court held that the petitioners as readers and contributors had locus standi to apply under Article 17, but the validity of the ban under emergency restrictions was decisive. Since the ban was lawful under Article 15(7), the petitioners' claims failed. The Court also expressed skepticism about allowing readers to claim rights that would effectively extend to the entire literate public.
principles_established: Freedom of speech and expression includes the right of the recipient to receive information.
Readers and contributors have locus standi under Article 17 to claim violations of fundamental rights.
The fundamental rights of recipients are subject to the same restrictions as those of publishers.
A non-citizen publisher has no fundamental right to publish, limiting the standing of readers.
The Court is cautious about extending locus standi to an amorphous public of readers.
precedents_cited: Dr. Neville Fernando and Others v. Liyanage and Others
Eleko v. Officer Administering the Government of Nigeria (1931) AC 662

outcome.holding: The Court held that the petitioners had locus standi under Article 17 as readers and contributors, but since the ban was lawful under Article 15(7), their claims failed and the applications were dismissed.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 17 governs the right to apply to the Supreme Court for violations of fundamental rights, which was central to the Court's consideration of the petitioners' standing and ability to bring the case.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The Court recognized that the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression includes the freedom of the recipient, thus granting locus standi to readers and contributors under Article 17, but ultimately dismissed the claims due to lawful restrictions under Article 15(7).
